svg.title: Reading a blood gas in four steps
svg.desc: Four steps across the top. Step one, read the pH: below 7.35 is acidemia, above 7.45 is alkalemia. Step two, decide which variable explains it: if the carbon dioxide tension moves the same way as the pH disturbance the disorder is respiratory, and if bicarbonate does, it is metabolic. Step three, check whether the compensation is the expected size, using the formulas given; a compensation outside the predicted range means a mixed disorder. Step four, for a metabolic acidosis compute the anion gap as sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate, normally eight to twelve. Below that, a two by two grid of the four primary disorders. Respiratory acidosis: the primary change is a rise in carbon dioxide tension from hypoventilation, pH falls below 7.35, and the kidney compensates by retaining bicarbonate over two to five days; causes include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, opioid overdose and neuromuscular disease. Respiratory alkalosis: carbon dioxide tension falls from hyperventilation, pH rises above 7.45, and the kidney compensates by excreting bicarbonate over days; causes include anxiety, altitude, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate toxicity and pregnancy. Metabolic acidosis: bicarbonate falls, pH falls, and the lungs compensate within minutes by hyperventilating, which is Kussmaul breathing; a high anion gap points to the MUDPILES causes and a normal anion gap to diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis or a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Metabolic alkalosis: bicarbonate rises, pH rises, and the lungs compensate by hypoventilating, though hypoxic drive limits how far; causes include vomiting, loop and thiazide diuretics, and hyperaldosteronism. A panel gives the expected compensations: for metabolic acidosis Winter's formula, expected carbon dioxide tension equals one and a half times bicarbonate plus eight, give or take two; for metabolic alkalosis carbon dioxide rises about nought point seven millimetres of mercury per unit rise in bicarbonate; for acute respiratory acidosis bicarbonate rises about one per ten millimetres of mercury and for chronic about three and a half; for acute respiratory alkalosis bicarbonate falls about two per ten and for chronic about five. A worked case follows: a twenty-two year old with type one diabetes, pH 7.10, carbon dioxide tension 20, bicarbonate 6, sodium 138, chloride 100. Step one, acidemia. Step two, bicarbonate is low, so metabolic acidosis. Step three, Winter's formula predicts fifteen to nineteen and the measured value is twenty, just outside, hinting at a mild concurrent respiratory acidosis. Step four, the anion gap is thirty-two, which is high, pointing to the ketoacids of diabetic ketoacidosis.
svg.text: Reading a blood gas in four steps
Normal: pH 7.40 · pCO₂ 40 mmHg · HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L. Every disorder is a deviation in one of the last two, and a partial correction in the other.
Is the compensation the right size?
Use the formulas below. Outside the
anxiety · altitude · PE · early salicylate · pregnancy
high AG: MUDPILES · normal AG: diarrhoea, RTA, CA inhibitor
compensation: lungs hypoventilate — limited by hypoxic drive
alkalosis: pCO₂ ↑ ~0.7 per 1 mEq/L ↑HCO₃⁻. Respiratory acidosis: HCO₃⁻
pH 7.10 · pCO₂ 20 · HCO₃⁻ 6 · Na⁺ 138 · Cl⁻ 100. (1) acidemia. (2)
HCO₃⁻ low → metabolic acidosis. (3) Winter's predicts 15–19; measured
20 sits just outside — a hint of mild concurrent respiratory acidosis.
The one thing compensation never does
It never overshoots, and it never fully corrects the pH in a simple disorder. So a normal pH with two clearly abnormal variables is
not a well-compensated single disorder — it is two opposing disorders at once. And compensation always moves the second variable in
the same direction as the first: both up, or both down.
